sourceNotes: Seeded from MCS roleplay performance indicators and marketing cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: MCS event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the marketing cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: Price per thousand impressions that actually rendered in view, so it is computed as the served CPM divided by the viewability rate — a $10 CPM delivered at 50% viewability really costs $20 per thousand seen.
terms.whyItMatters: A media-buying roleplay that asks which of two display placements is cheaper is decided on this number, not the quoted rate: the cheaper served CPM loses once its viewability rate is applied.

terms.definition: Revenue or spend restated onto a per-thousand-impressions basis — earnings divided by impressions, times 1,000 — so a CPC, CPA or flat-fee buy can be compared against a CPM buy on one scale. $300 on 200,000 impressions is a $1.50 eCPM.
terms.whyItMatters: When a client hands you a mixed plan of CPC search, CPA affiliate and CPM display and asks which line to cut, converting all three to eCPM is the only way to rank them in a presentation.

terms.definition: Video spend divided by the number of plays that reached 100% completion, which prices only finished views — unlike cost per view, where a platform may bill at 30 seconds or at the end of a shorter ad, so the two metrics can differ several-fold on the same flight.
terms.whyItMatters: A pre-roll buy judged on CPV can look efficient while most viewers skip; the exam question that asks why a video campaign with a low CPV delivered no message recall is answered with completion rate and CPCV.

terms.definition: The counting threshold an impression must clear to be billed as seen: at least 50% of the ad's pixels in the viewport for at least one continuous second for display, and 50% of pixels for two continuous seconds for video, with large-format units allowed 30% of pixels for one second.
terms.whyItMatters: In a roleplay where a publisher and an agency argue over an invoice, quoting the pixel-and-duration threshold decides which impressions are billable rather than leaving it to opinion.

terms.definition: Gap between the publisher's impression count and the agency's third-party ad server count, caused by latency, blocked tags and count-on-request versus count-on-render logic; roughly 10% is the accepted tolerance, and inside it the buy is reconciled and billed on the third-party number.
terms.whyItMatters: A trafficking question that gives two impression totals is testing whether you know the 10% tolerance and which count pays; above it the advertiser withholds and asks for an investigation or a makegood.

terms.definition: The lookback period inside which a conversion is still credited to a prior ad click or view — commonly 7 days after a click and 1 day after a view. Lengthening it moves conversions into the campaign and lowers reported cost per acquisition without a dollar of spend changing.
terms.whyItMatters: When a client claims a channel's CPA improved month over month, the first thing to check in a presentation is whether the window was widened; the exam tests that the metric moved, not the media.

terms.definition: A U-shaped credit split that assigns 40% of a conversion's value to the first touch, 40% to the last touch and divides the remaining 20% across every middle touch — deliberately rewarding the channel that created awareness as well as the one that closed.
terms.whyItMatters: Awareness media always looks worthless under last-click reporting; recommending this split with its 40/20/40 weights is how a competitor defends an upper-funnel line item in a budget roleplay.

terms.definition: Credit weighted by recency on an exponential curve, typically a seven-day half-life: a touchpoint one week before the conversion earns half the credit of one on the conversion day, and two weeks out a quarter of it.
terms.whyItMatters: For a long consideration purchase, choosing between this model and a U-shaped split changes which channel the budget follows — a standard media-planning defense in a Marketing Communications roleplay.

terms.definition: The average number of people tuned to a station for at least five minutes within a given 15-minute block; dividing it by the market population and multiplying by 100 yields the AQH rating, which is the rating point a radio buy is actually priced against.
terms.whyItMatters: Radio schedules are costed as cost per point, and the point comes from this five-minute rule — a broadcast buying question is unsolvable without converting AQH persons into an AQH rating first.

terms.definition: The count of different people who tuned in for at least five minutes anywhere in a daypart, each counted once no matter how often they returned — so it measures reach, and dividing it by average quarter-hour persons gives turnover, the number of audiences the station cycles through.
terms.whyItMatters: A station selling on a big cume and a buyer costing the schedule on AQH are quoting two different numbers; the exam asks which one supports a reach goal and which one supports frequency.

terms.definition: Total exposures a schedule delivers with duplication left in — gross rating points times the universe divided by 100 — so the figure always exceeds net reach, and reach times average frequency reproduces it exactly.
terms.whyItMatters: Given GRPs and a market population, this conversion is the single most common media-math item on a marketing communications exam, and it is also how a plan is restated for a client who thinks in people, not points.

terms.definition: The share of a vehicle's audience that falls in the target divided by that group's share of the general population, times 100 — 100 is parity, 120 means the vehicle over-delivers the target by 20%, and below 100 the buy is paying for waste.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing between two magazines with similar CPMs comes down to this index, and a competitor who cannot say what an index of 85 means will recommend the cheaper, wronger book.

terms.definition: The out-of-home audience figure for a single unit — the average number of people per day passing it with a reasonable opportunity to see the face — and it is the denominator that turns a panel's monthly rate into a comparable CPM.
terms.whyItMatters: An outdoor proposal quotes a flat monthly price per board; converting each board to a CPM through this circulation figure is the only way to rank locations in a media-buying roleplay.

terms.definition: The out-of-home weight level named for the share of the market it covers daily: a #50 showing buys enough faces to deliver daily impressions equal to 50% of the market population, a #100 delivers 100%, and the number is a daily GRP level rather than a count of boards.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor who quotes '25 posters' has told you nothing; asking for the showing level converts the offer into daily GRPs your plan can be held to, which is exactly what a judge listens for.

terms.definition: A print comparison figure computed as the cost of one agate line multiplied by 1,000,000 and divided by circulation, which restates newspapers of wildly different sizes as one price per line per million readers.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to justify buying the smaller paper, a competitor who shows a lower milline rate has proved the cheaper audience; comparing raw line rates between papers proves nothing.

terms.definition: The circulation or impression figure a publisher contractually guarantees and is independently audited against; missing it obliges the publisher to rebate the advertiser or supply replacement weight, and rates are set on the guarantee rather than on actual delivery.
terms.whyItMatters: When a magazine's audited circulation comes in under the guarantee, knowing the remedy is a rebate or a makegood is what turns an advertiser's complaint into a settled negotiation in a roleplay.

terms.definition: Replacement weight supplied free when a schedule under-delivers its guaranteed rating points or impressions, or when a unit runs wrong — settled in equivalent audience delivery in a comparable daypart, not in a cash refund of the dollars spent.
terms.whyItMatters: A station that delivers 180 of 200 guaranteed GRPs owes the missing 20 points, and the roleplay tests whether you negotiate the replacement in equivalent audience rather than accepting cheap late-night filler.

terms.definition: The traditional media compensation of 15% of gross billing retained by the agency, so the net cost owed the medium is the gross times 0.85 — and grossing a net price back up requires multiplying by 1.1765, because 15% of gross equals 17.65% of net.
terms.whyItMatters: A quoted net rate and a quoted gross rate for the same spot differ by that 17.65% markup; a budget question that mixes the two is unsolvable unless you convert, and clients notice which way you rounded.

terms.definition: The federal rule entitling a legally qualified candidate to a station's cheapest rate for the same class and time period, during the 45 days before a primary and the 60 days before a general election, regardless of the volume any commercial advertiser bought to earn that rate.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains why commercial inventory gets preempted and repriced every fall election season — a scheduling conflict a competitor must be able to explain to a client whose flight lands inside the window.

terms.definition: Federal requirement that a commercial not be transmitted louder than the program it accompanies, enforced not by opinion but by measured average loudness under the ATSC A/85 recommended practice, whose United States target is roughly -24 LKFS.
terms.whyItMatters: A spot rejected at station QC for loudness is a production problem with a numeric fix, and knowing the target keeps a Marketing Communications competitor from promising a client a re-edit that will fail again.

terms.definition: Statutory caps on commercial matter inside programming aimed at children 12 and under — 10.5 minutes per hour on weekends and 12 minutes per hour on weekdays — enforced alongside bans on host-selling and on program-length commercials.
terms.whyItMatters: A client wanting to advertise a toy inside a kids block is constrained by these per-hour minutes and by who may deliver the message, and an ethics-flavored exam item turns on the exact figures.

terms.definition: A private federal suit under Section 43(a) letting one competitor sue another over false or misleading commercial advertising, requiring a false or misleading statement of fact in interstate commerce, deception that is material to purchase, and resulting injury — with injunctions, the defendant's profits and damages available, and no FTC involvement at all.
terms.whyItMatters: When a rival's comparative ad misstates your client's product, the answer is not to file with the FTC but to name this claim and its elements — a distinction that separates a prepared roleplay from a vague one.

terms.definition: The evidentiary bar an objective advertising claim must meet — tests or studies run by qualified people using procedures generally accepted in the field, typically at least one well-controlled randomized human clinical trial for a health claim — and it has to exist before the ad runs, not be assembled after a challenge.
terms.whyItMatters: A client who wants 'clinically proven' in the headline is asking for a claim that needs this file on hand at launch; explaining the prior-substantiation timing is the professional answer in an ethics roleplay.

terms.definition: The FTC standard for qualifying information: unavoidable, delivered in the same medium as the claim it modifies, placed close to that claim, and worded so an ordinary consumer understands it — a hyperlink, a hashtag, or fine print past the fold does not satisfy it.
terms.whyItMatters: Influencer and native placements live or die on this test, so a competitor briefing a creator has to say where the disclosure goes, not merely that one is required.

terms.definition: A scheduling philosophy that spreads weight into continuous weekly presence chasing one-plus weekly reach, instead of concentrating a burst to build three-plus frequency, on the reasoning that the exposure nearest a purchase decision does the persuading.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the argument for turning a client's four-week blitz into a year of light weekly coverage, and a judge expects the reach-versus-frequency trade to be named out loud.

terms.definition: The binding contract behind a media buy, specifying flight dates, units, placements, rates, targeting, the delivery guarantee and the cancellation terms — it is the document a delivery dispute is settled against, and verbal confirmations are not.
terms.whyItMatters: When a publisher under-delivers, the remedy comes from this paperwork, so a roleplay about a shorted campaign is really a question about what the buyer wrote down before the flight started.

terms.definition: Planning shorthand for average frequency — total exposures divided by net reach — counting chances to encounter the message rather than proven attention, which is why it is an upper bound on what the audience really absorbed.
terms.whyItMatters: A plan promising a client four OTS is promising exposures, not four people persuaded; distinguishing the two protects a competitor from over-claiming in a presentation.

terms.definition: Targeted messages sent straight to individuals by mail, email, or phone.
terms.whyItMatters: Direct marketing allows personalized, measurable, one-to-one engagement.

terms.definition: Deliberately putting back the duplicated columns that normalization removed, trading write cost and update anomalies for read speed: one wide table answers a report with zero joins, but a customer who changes her surname must now be rewritten in every row that copied it, and any row missed is a silent contradiction.
terms.whyItMatters: A reporting-performance roleplay asks why the analytics table repeats the region name in a million rows; the defensible answer is the read-versus-write trade-off, not sloppy design.

terms.definition: Section 102(c) of the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act forbids conditioning a written warranty on the buyer's use of a branded part or an authorized service center unless the warrantor supplies that part or service free of charge or holds an FTC waiver — so an independent repair shop cannot by itself void coverage, and neither can failing to mail back a registration card, because the purchase date is what proves the claim. A service contract sold for separate consideration is not a warranty and never falls under this rule.
terms.whyItMatters: An automotive- or electronics-services roleplay where a guest was told their warranty died because they used an outside mechanic is scored on interpreting the policy correctly to the customer rather than repeating the store's line.

terms.definition: Models trustworthiness as credibility plus reliability plus intimacy, all divided by self-orientation — so visibly acting in your own interest divides away everything the other three terms earn. Credibility is about words, reliability about repeated actions over time, and intimacy about safety in disclosure, which is why a person can be believable and still not be trusted.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on rebuilding a client or coworker relationship is scored on lowering the self-orientation term — leading with their problem — rather than on producing more credentials.

terms.definition: Divides the running cumulative forecast error by the mean absolute deviation to test whether misses are random noise or one-sided drift; a value wandering past ±4 says the model is systematically off and must be re-fit rather than nudged, while a value oscillating around zero says the error is noise and the model should be left alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast-control questions supply a cumulative error and a MAD and want both the ratio and the keep-or-refit call against the limit, not a general remark that the forecast looks wrong.

terms.definition: Enforces a promise that never had a bargained-for exchange behind it when four elements line up: a clear and definite promise, the promisor's reasonable expectation that it would induce reliance, actual detrimental reliance by the promisee, and injustice avoidable only by enforcement. Recovery is usually capped at what reliance cost, not the full expectancy a consideration-backed contract would deliver.
terms.whyItMatters: Contract exam items about a supplier who withdrew a quoted price after the buyer already used it to bid a job test this doctrine, not consideration.

terms.definition: The percentage of one brand's national sales made in a market divided by that market's percentage of national population, times 100; read against the category index it sorts markets into four actions — high BDI with low CDI means a strong brand in a weak category, while low BDI with high CDI is the classic opportunity market where the category sells well and the brand does not, and both indexes below 100 argues for withdrawal.
terms.whyItMatters: The paired index read is the standard answer to a roleplay asking which market to defend and which to invest in; giving one index without the other gets a follow-up you cannot answer.

terms.definition: The specific benefit that makes a product distinctly better than rivals'.
terms.whyItMatters: A clear USP gives customers a compelling reason to choose the product.

terms.definition: Total media spend divided by completed conversions rather than by clicks — $800 producing 16 purchases is $50, even though that same $800 buying 3,200 clicks made cost per click look like $0.25. Rising here with a flat cost per click means the landing page, not the media, is failing.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item showing cheap clicks and expensive customers is testing whether the competitor can locate the failure downstream of the ad, and a roleplay client who wants to cut the ad budget is usually the one who needs the page fixed.

terms.definition: Splitting one table's rows horizontally across several servers by a key, so four servers each carry about 25% of the rows and the system gains write capacity and room. Replication does the opposite — it copies 100% of the rows onto every server, buying read capacity and failover but not one byte of extra space.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on a database that has outgrown its server asks which approach fixes it; recommending more copies of a table that no longer fits is the trap the judge is watching for.

terms.definition: The activities a business uses to build satisfaction, trust, and loyalty.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong customer relations support repeat business and reputation.

terms.definition: A short opening section of a report that distills key findings and recommendations.
terms.whyItMatters: Written events reward a crisp, decision-ready summary.

terms.definition: The work of managing your own feelings to satisfy an employer's display rules — the face the job requires — and it is performed two ways: surface acting, which puts on the expression while the underlying feeling is unchanged, and deep acting, which alters the felt emotion itself. Surface acting is the strategy repeatedly tied to higher exhaustion and turnover; deep acting is not.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on staffing a long shift of difficult interactions is scored on recognizing that requiring a constant smile is a real cost to be scheduled around, not a free instruction.

terms.definition: Scores every step of a forecasting process by the accuracy points it adds over the naive baseline — baseline MAPE 20%, statistical model 17%, sales-team override 19% — so the model step is worth +3 points and the override is worth −2 and should be removed from the process rather than coached.
terms.whyItMatters: Process-improvement items ask which forecasting step to cut, and the negative-value step is the answer; it is also the numeric way a plan review argues that field overrides are hurting the number instead of helping it.

terms.definition: Distinct customers who bought at least once in a period divided by the total defined target population, as a percentage — 40,000 buyers out of a 500,000-person target is 8% — which counts buyers, not units or dollars; that is exactly what separates it from market share, so a brand can raise share by selling more to the same people while its penetration does not move at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Growth roleplays hinge on whether the plan should recruit new buyers or sell more to current ones, and this is the number that tells the judge you know which lever you chose.

terms.definition: The first 2.5% of a market to buy something new -- venturesome, able to absorb a failed purchase, and often socially outside the mainstream, which limits their influence; the early adopters who follow are the next 13.5% and carry the opinion leadership that actually moves the majority.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product roleplays ask who to target at launch; quoting the 2.5% band and then explaining why that group cannot spread adoption alone is what separates the top scores.

terms.definition: Customer recommendations and referrals that spread opinions about a product.
terms.whyItMatters: Word-of-mouth builds organic advocacy and trust beyond paid ads.

terms.definition: Export price index divided by import price index, times 100. A country whose export prices climb 6% while import prices climb 2% moves from 100 to about 104 and can buy more foreign goods per unit shipped; a commodity exporter watching prices slide sees the figure drop even with export volume flat.
terms.whyItMatters: Trade-alliance and global-environment questions ask who gained from a shift in world prices, and the ratio of the two indexes settles it.

terms.definition: The result that a distributed data store can hold at most two of three guarantees — consistency, availability, and tolerance of a network partition. Because a partition is a fact of networks rather than a design option, the live choice is only between the other two: refuse the read and stay correct, or answer it and risk handing back stale data.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why a cloud inventory system showed two stores different stock counts during an outage, the competitor has to name the trade-off the vendor chose instead of calling it a bug.

terms.definition: The total profit a business expects from a customer over the whole relationship.
terms.whyItMatters: CLV guides how much to invest in retention and service.

terms.definition: Fisher and Ury's method built on four rules — separate the people from the problem, focus on interests instead of stated positions, invent options for mutual gain before deciding anything, and insist on an objective standard for the outcome. A position is what a party demands; the interest is why they want it, and only the interest can usually be satisfied in more than one way.
terms.whyItMatters: Negotiation roleplays are scored on surfacing the reason behind a demand and offering two options that meet it, which positional haggling over one number cannot produce.

terms.definition: The geographic zone a location actually draws customers from, mapped as rings: the primary ring supplies roughly 60-75% of customers, the secondary another 15-25%, and the fringe the scattered remainder. It sets the population a site's forecast is allowed to count.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-selection and retail-expansion cases give customer ZIP-code counts and ask how far the draw reaches; forecasting against the whole metropolitan population instead of the primary ring inflates every downstream number.

terms.definition: The core marketing activities such as pricing, promotion, selling, and distribution.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors organize their analysis around which marketing functions a decision touches.

terms.definition: Paying a loan off through fixed installments split between interest and principal, with the interest share largest at the start and shrinking every payment.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask why an early mortgage payment barely reduces the balance; the amortization split is the reason, not a fee.

terms.definition: The 13.5% of buyers who follow the innovators -- respected opinion leaders inside the mainstream whose endorsement decides whether an item reaches the 34% early majority; innovators, the first 2.5%, buy sooner but sit too far outside the group to persuade it.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion plans for a launch are scored on targeting the group that others watch; naming the 13.5% band and its opinion-leader role answers the indicator directly.

terms.definition: Revenue attributable to a campaign divided by what that campaign cost: $40,000 of revenue on $10,000 of spend is 4.0. It differs from return on investment, which subtracts cost of goods and the spend itself before dividing, so a 4.0 here is still a losing campaign at a 20% gross margin.
terms.whyItMatters: A client presenting a campaign as a four-to-one success is the setup for this distinction; the competitor is expected to ask for the margin before agreeing the campaign made money.

terms.definition: Keep three copies of the data on two different media types with one copy held off-site; the arithmetic is the whole point, because a single fire cannot reach the off-site copy, a single failing drive model cannot corrupt the second medium, and one ransomware blast radius cannot encrypt all three at once.
terms.whyItMatters: A storage roleplay about a flooded back office is graded on stating the counts, since answering 'we back up nightly' does not survive the follow-up about where the backup was sitting.

terms.definition: A relationship of mutual understanding and trust between a business and its customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Building rapport raises trust and the odds of repeat business.

terms.definition: Short for best alternative to a negotiated agreement: the course of action you would actually take if these talks failed, which is what sets real bargaining power. It is not the price target and not the reservation price — the reservation price is the worst deal still worth accepting, derived from the alternative — and improving the outside option raises your power even if nothing at the table changes.
terms.whyItMatters: A supplier or salary negotiation roleplay is scored on the candidate knowing their walk-away option and estimating the other side's before conceding.

terms.definition: The stepped route a complaint travels under a collective bargaining agreement — usually the immediate supervisor, then department management with a union steward, then a company-wide review, ending in binding arbitration by a neutral third party whose decision both sides accepted in advance. Each step carries its own filing deadline, and missing one can forfeit the claim regardless of merit.
terms.whyItMatters: A union-workplace roleplay is scored on routing the complaint through the contract's steps rather than settling it informally with the employee.

terms.definition: Divides the standard deviation of period demand by its mean to grade how forecastable a series is: under about 0.25 a single point forecast is dependable, and above roughly 0.50 the item is erratic enough that the plan must carry a range and a buffer instead of one number.
terms.whyItMatters: Planning questions ask which item deserves a statistical forecast and which needs judgment plus safety stock; the ratio decides it, and the threshold is the part of the item being tested.

terms.definition: The top rung of the three-stage loyalty ladder: at recognition the buyer merely knows the mark, at preference the buyer chooses it but accepts a substitute when it is out of stock, and at insistence the buyer will leave the store or delay the purchase rather than take another brand — the only stage that lets a firm hold price through a competitor's promotion.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays ask what a strong brand is actually worth; naming the three stages and the out-of-stock behavior that separates preference from insistence is what earns the point.

terms.definition: Measures how closely the lines relate in production, distribution, and end use -- something neither width nor depth can show: two firms each carrying 4 lines and 40 items differ sharply when one sells only refrigerated foods through grocers and the other sells food, tires, and insurance.
terms.whyItMatters: Diversification questions ask whether a proposed line fits; the scoring point is that the new line shares plants or channels with the existing ones, not that it sounds related.

terms.definition: An ad's key elements — headline, copy, visuals, call to action, and branding.
terms.whyItMatters: Each component ensures the ad communicates its message persuasively.

terms.definition: Striping with parity distributed across at least 3 disks: usable capacity is (n−1)/n of the raw total, so four 2 TB disks give 6 TB rather than 8, and exactly one disk may fail with no data lost. The exposure is the rebuild — a second failure while the array reconstructs the first destroys everything on it.
terms.whyItMatters: A storage-purchase roleplay asks how much of a quoted 8 TB array the business actually gets and how many drive failures it survives; both numbers come straight from the level.

terms.definition: The square root of (2 x annual demand x cost per order) divided by annual holding cost per unit — the single order size where rising carrying cost and falling ordering cost cross and total cost bottoms out.
terms.whyItMatters: An operations roleplay that asks you to cut the cost of holding stock is answered with this trade-off, not with 'order less': you must say that ordering more often lowers carrying cost but raises order cost, and name the quantity where the two balance.

terms.definition: Contacts fully resolved on the first interaction divided by total contacts handled — 1,200 of 1,500 is 80%. A case that is transferred to a second agent or reopened later counts as a failure even if it is solved the same day, which is why it moves in the opposite direction from average handle time whenever agents rush callers off the line.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on service improvement, the fix a competitor proposes has to raise this number; trimming call length by promising a callback lowers it.

terms.definition: Over-weighting a person's character and under-weighting their circumstances when explaining someone else's behavior — the late colleague is careless rather than stuck behind an accident. Its mirror image applied to oneself is the self-serving bias, and together the pair make an appraisal reward good luck and punish bad context.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item asking why a supervisor rates a rep poorly after a territory loses its largest account expects this bias by name, and roleplays on fair evaluation reward asking about conditions before judging the person.

terms.definition: Personal income for an area minus personal tax payments — the disposable dollars residents can actually spend, not gross earnings. It is the income term inside a buying power index, which weights it against the area's population and retail sales.
terms.whyItMatters: Territory and market-selection items give gross income for two cities and expect the after-tax spendable figure to drive the ranking, because a high-tax market supports less spending than its wage level suggests.

terms.definition: The added value a strong, well-known brand name gives a product.
terms.whyItMatters: Brand equity explains why customers pay more for, and stay loyal to, established brands.

terms.definition: A purchase for which buyers accept no substitute and will pass closer outlets to reach one brand -- insistence, not preference; a shopping good is one buyers compare on price, quality, and style across several stores and will happily switch brands on to save money.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution questions follow from this classification: specialty goods justify exclusive distribution and few outlets, while shopping goods need enough outlets for comparison to happen.

terms.definition: Member-governed body that publishes a code of ethics, administers credentialing exams and sets practice standards for a field — the AICPA for accountants, SHRM for HR professionals. A labor union may cover overlapping workers but bargains collectively over wages and conditions; an association negotiates nothing and its only sanction is revoking the credential.
terms.whyItMatters: The accounting roleplay that asks what a professional organization does for a member is scored on services and enforcement, and confusing it with a union loses the item.

terms.definition: An auction in which the winner pays one increment above the runner-up's bid rather than the amount they themselves bid, so a $4.00 bid beating a $2.50 bid clears at $2.51 — which is why bidding true value can never cost more than that value is worth.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital-buying items ask why an advertiser should enter its real maximum instead of shading the bid down; the mechanic, not the strategy, is the answer, and competitors who guess pay-what-you-bid get it backwards.

terms.definition: Mirrored pairs that are then striped: usable capacity is exactly half the raw total, so the same four 2 TB disks give 4 TB instead of 6, but the array survives one failure in every pair and rebuilds by copying a single disk rather than recomputing parity from all the rest.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing two quotes for the same four drives, the competitor has to trade 2 TB of capacity against a faster, safer rebuild — a judge expects the capacity figure said out loud.

terms.definition: Talk time plus hold time plus after-call work, divided by contacts handled — 6 minutes of talk, 1 minute of hold and 3 minutes of wrap-up across 40 calls averages 10 minutes. Leaving wrap-up out of the numerator is the standard error, and it makes every staffing model built on the figure understaff the queue.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing math in a peak-demand hospitality or call-center roleplay starts here, and exam items expect the wrap-up term to be inside the average.

terms.definition: Scott's grid crossing caring personally with challenging directly: high on both is candor, caring without challenging is ruinous empathy that withholds the correction that would have helped, challenging without caring is obnoxious aggression, and neither is manipulative insincerity. The named failure most managers actually commit is the first, not harshness.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a well-liked employee is quietly underperforming is scored on delivering the specific correction, since softening it to protect the relationship is the graded mistake.

terms.definition: Splits a revenue miss into three computed pieces that must add back to the total gap: price variance = (actual price − planned price) × actual units; volume variance = (actual units − planned units) × planned price; mix variance = the shift in each product's share of total units valued at planned prices.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-review items give planned and actual price, units and product split and expect all three figures; answering that sales came in soft without the decomposition is exactly what the rubric withholds credit for.

terms.definition: The advisory power of specialists such as legal, HR, or IT to recommend and to be consulted, without the power to order action in another department; line authority is the direct command relationship over subordinates who produce the firm's goods or services.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe an HR manager whose hiring recommendation a plant manager overrode and ask which authority type each held.

terms.definition: Attributes a brand must match well enough for buyers to accept it as a legitimate member of the category — a car that is safe, a bank that clears deposits — which buy entry and win no preference at all; the attributes that win preference are points of difference, and because parity is a threshold rather than a scale, money spent beating a rival on a parity attribute returns nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking where to invest a product-improvement budget is a parity-versus-difference question; spending to over-deliver on a category minimum is the error the judge is watching for.

terms.definition: Moves a new product through fixed stages separated by go/kill reviews with written criteria, so a project can die at any gate -- screening, business analysis, development, testing, launch; the long-standing planning ratio is roughly 7 serious ideas entering for every 1 commercial success.
terms.whyItMatters: Development roleplays ask what happens between an idea and a launch; the scoring point is that each gate can kill the project, not that the stages happen in order.

terms.definition: Coordinating all promotion for one consistent message across channels.
terms.whyItMatters: Consistency across touchpoints reinforces the message and maximizes impact.

terms.definition: Written with dollar signs as $A$1, it pins both the column and the row so the address does not shift when the formula is copied down or across; a relative reference such as A1 moves with the copy, and a mixed reference such as $A1 or A$1 freezes only the half carrying the dollar sign.
terms.whyItMatters: Spreadsheet items give a tax rate in one cell and ask why copying the formula produced zeros further down the column; the missing dollar signs are the graded answer.

terms.definition: A mindset committed to meeting customer needs and providing quality help.
terms.whyItMatters: It helps employees deliver consistent, customer-focused interactions.

terms.definition: Sales a new channel takes from an existing one rather than creating: a direct site booking $500,000 while dealer revenue falls $400,000 is 80 percent cannibalized and contributes only $100,000 of truly incremental volume. Because the incumbent channel's margin is usually different, the right comparison is incremental CONTRIBUTION, not incremental revenue.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a company store or direct site is scored on subtracting the incumbent channel's lost sales; presenting the new channel's gross revenue as growth is the classic error.

terms.definition: Gable's strongest of four ways to answer someone's good news, formed by crossing active with passive and constructive with destructive: responding actively and constructively means asking questions that let the person relive the event, while passive-constructive is a flat nice job, active-destructive points out the downside, and passive-destructive changes the subject. Only the first strengthens the relationship.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays on recognizing a team member's contribution are scored on a specific, curious response in the moment rather than a generic congratulation or a deferred award.

terms.definition: Isolates the profit effect of selling a different blend than planned: for each item, (its actual share of total units − its planned share) × total actual units × that item's planned contribution per unit, summed across the line — so a firm can hit its unit target exactly and still miss profit by shifting volume onto the thinner-margin product.
terms.whyItMatters: Shortfall questions where total units met plan are solved with this term alone, and it is the numeric case for paying sales incentives on contribution rather than on units sold.

terms.definition: Attributes buyers strongly associate with one brand, rate favorably, and believe no competitor delivers as well — all three conditions, not just the first — which is what makes them the reason to choose it, unlike points of parity, which only qualify the brand for the consideration set; once rivals match a claimed difference it has quietly become a parity attribute and stops moving share even though the advertising still runs.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to identify what sets a company apart, a competitor who names a feature every rival also offers has named a parity attribute and will be corrected on the spot.

terms.definition: Portable, shorter-lived business goods bought routinely by middle managers and written off over a few years -- hand tools, laptops, forklifts; an installation is the major capital asset such as a plant or a production line, approved by top management on a multi-year capital budget.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business selling roleplays are scored on calling on the right buyer: the pair differs by who signs, so pitching an installation to a department manager is a scoring miss.

terms.definition: The Media Rating Council standard that counts a display impression only when at least 50% of its pixels hold the screen for one continuous second — two continuous seconds for video — so a campaign can serve 1,000,000 impressions and have only 600,000 of them count.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay where the client is billed for impressions the audience never had a chance to see is resolved by this standard, and exam items use the gap between served and counted impressions to test whether the competitor knows the threshold.

terms.definition: Word-of-mouth conversation about a brand across social and community channels.
terms.whyItMatters: Monitoring buzz reveals brand perception and emerging issues early.

terms.definition: The bit count of a cryptographic key, which cannot be compared across algorithm families: a 256-bit symmetric key doubles in strength with each added bit, while a 2048-bit RSA key rests on the difficulty of factoring and rates at only about 112 bits of equivalent strength. The far bigger number is the weaker key.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-security roleplay asks whether a supplier advertising 2048-bit encryption beats one advertising 256-bit; reading the digits alone gives the wrong recommendation.

terms.definition: The share of contacts answered inside a stated number of seconds, written as a pair — the industry default target is 80% answered within 20 seconds, and the other 20% may wait any length of time at all. That blind spot is why it is reported alongside average speed of answer rather than instead of it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks a competitor to set a staffing target for a holiday peak wants this pair of numbers, not a promise to answer quickly.

terms.definition: Letting one strong impression, often a single outstanding trait, lift every unrelated rating for the same person; its inverse, the horns effect, drags them all down from one bad impression. In an appraisal it shows up as suspiciously uniform scores across dimensions that ought to vary, and the standard counter is rating every employee on one dimension at a time before moving to the next.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that shows an evaluation form with identical scores in every category is testing this, and an HR roleplay on fixing a review process is scored on the dimension-by-dimension fix.

terms.definition: The average signed error across periods — actual minus forecast with the plus and minus signs kept — so persistent over-forecasting shows up as a running negative. It measures direction, where MAPE measures size, and a plan can post a respectable MAPE while drifting the same way every single month.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast-review items give a run of months that miss high every time and ask what is wrong with the method; the answer is a systematic error in the assumptions, not random noise.

terms.definition: The percentage of total sales in a market captured by one business or product.
terms.whyItMatters: Market share quantifies competitive position and the payoff of a growth strategy.

terms.definition: Fixed costs / contribution margin per unit - the volume at which total revenue and total cost meet and profit is exactly zero. Dividing fixed costs by the contribution margin ratio instead answers the same question in sales dollars, which is the form used when a firm sells a mix of products.
terms.whyItMatters: An entrepreneurship written event has to show the venture's break-even volume before a judge will give credit for the financial section of the plan.

terms.definition: Applies stated go/no-go criteria to drop weak concepts before money is spent, and guards against two opposite errors -- a drop-error that kills a winner and a go-error that carries a loser into costly development; idea generation, by contrast, deliberately withholds all judgment to maximize the count.
terms.whyItMatters: A brainstorming roleplay is scored badly if you evaluate while generating; competitors must say which stage they are in and which error that stage is trying to avoid.

terms.definition: Marketing through online channels such as social media, email, and search.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital promotion reaches audiences efficiently with measurable results.

terms.definition: Two different inputs producing the same fixed-length digest, which has to be possible because inputs are unlimited and digests are not. A 256-bit digest has 2^256 possible outputs, but the birthday bound puts an attacker's expected work at about 2^128 attempts — the square root, not the full space — which is why a 128-bit digest is retired and a 256-bit one is not.
terms.whyItMatters: An information-ethics item asks why a system that stores digests instead of files can still be attacked; the square-root shortcut, not the digest length on the label, is the reasoning.

terms.definition: Contacts that disconnect while waiting divided by contacts offered — 90 hang-ups out of 3,000 offered is 3%, and most centers exclude calls dropped inside the first 5 seconds as misdials before reporting it. Under 5% is the common acceptance band, and the number rises non-linearly once average wait passes the caller's patience threshold.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand over the offered and abandoned counts and expect both the percentage and the staffing conclusion drawn from it.

terms.definition: Deci and Ryan's account of motivation as three psychological needs — autonomy, competence and relatedness — plus a continuum running from purely external regulation through introjected and identified regulation to fully internalized motivation. Motivation is therefore a location on that continuum rather than an amount, and only the internalized end keeps working once the supervisor stops watching.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking why a bonus program stopped producing results, or a roleplay on motivating a team without extra budget, is scored on giving choice, competence feedback and belonging instead of raising the payout.

terms.definition: The sales-tax duty a seller picks up in a state where it owns no building and employs no one, triggered purely by volume — commonly $100,000 of sales or 200 separate transactions into that state in the current or prior year. Cross the threshold and the seller must register, collect and remit there; a purely online business is not exempt.
terms.whyItMatters: E-commerce selling items give a state-by-state sales table and ask where tax must now be collected; an expansion roleplay expects you to raise registration before recommending a push into a new state.

terms.definition: The percentage change in unit sales delivered by a one-percent change in advertising spending — 3% more volume on 10% more spend is 0.3 — and because measured values usually sit near 0.1 to 0.2, doubling the budget rarely comes close to doubling volume; compare it against price elasticity before choosing which lever to pull.
terms.whyItMatters: Budget-allocation items supply both elasticities and expect the higher-return lever chosen with the arithmetic shown; a plan that asks for more advertising without this number has no answer when the judge asks why not a price move instead.

terms.definition: A brand architecture in which the corporate name stays off the products and each brand carries its own separate equity — Procter & Gamble's Tide, Pampers and Gillette show no visible parent — which is the opposite of a branded house, where one master name fronts every offering; the trade-off is that a failure in one brand cannot contaminate the others, paid for by funding awareness separately for each name.
terms.whyItMatters: Corporate-branding roleplays ask whether a new line should carry the parent name; the answer turns on this architecture choice and the contamination risk it prices.

terms.definition: A finished business good that goes into another product and keeps its own identity there -- a car battery, a tire, a microchip; raw materials are processed until that identity is lost, and maintenance and repair supplies never enter the finished product at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Industrial product questions ask you to classify an input; the identity test decides it, and it also explains why component makers can advertise to the end consumer at all.

terms.definition: Clicks divided by impressions: 250 clicks on 125,000 impressions is 0.2%, which is an ordinary display result and a poor search result. The denominator is impressions served, not people reached, so the figure falls as frequency rises even when the creative is working.
terms.whyItMatters: Campaign-review roleplays hand over a rate that dropped week over week; the competitor is expected to check whether frequency rose before concluding the creative went stale.

terms.definition: A primary key spread across two or more columns, where uniqueness is broken only when every column in the key matches at once — a key on (student_id, course_id) lets the same student appear 6 times and the same course appear 300 times, but the pair exactly once.
terms.whyItMatters: Enrollment and order-line questions ask how many rows one student or one product may hold; the count comes from reading the columns in the key, not from any rule about the table.

terms.definition: Protection granted to original works of authorship such as writing, music, and art.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital content and creative works are critical assets in modern business.

terms.definition: The commitment a company makes about the value and experience it will deliver.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing the promise helps employees deliver a consistent experience.

terms.definition: Damping an emotion after it has already arrived by hiding its outward signs, rather than changing the interpretation that produced it. Because it is applied late, it leaves the physiological arousal fully intact, raises blood pressure in the person watching as well, and measurably impairs memory for what was said during the episode -- the opposite profile from cognitive reappraisal, which is applied early and carries none of those costs.
terms.whyItMatters: When a Human Resources Management Series judge asks how you would hold composure while an employee vents about a denied raise, an answer built on hiding what you felt names the strategy research links to worse recall of the conversation; the scoring answer reinterprets the outburst before it peaks.

terms.definition: Carries advertising effect forward as this week's effect = this week's spending effect + (retention rate × last week's carried effect); at a retention rate of 0.7 a flight that ends today still delivers 70% of its pull next week and 49% the week after, which is why a brand can stop spending and not lose sales immediately.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-scheduling questions ask whether a brand can go dark for a month, and this decay arithmetic answers it; it also fixes how long after a campaign ends a plan may still credit sales to that campaign.

terms.definition: Divides a market by activities, interests, opinions, values and lifestyle captured through AIO inventories, unlike demographic segmentation, which uses census-verifiable facts such as age, income and household size; two 34-year-olds each earning $60,000 fall in one demographic cell and can still land in opposite psychographic segments, which is why demographics alone cannot explain why one buys the premium line.
terms.whyItMatters: A market-planning roleplay that hands you a customer base and asks for a segmentation base is scored on naming the base and defending it against the other three; the usual failure is calling lifestyle data 'demographics'.

terms.definition: Places a pre-release version with outside customers doing real work in their own conditions, capturing failures no internal lab reproduces; alpha testing comes first and is run in-house by employees, so a beta's whole value is the uncontrolled use an alpha deliberately excludes.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a limited launch is scored on why outside users are needed before full production, not merely on saying the product will be tested.

terms.definition: Hofstede's 0-to-100 measure of how threatened a culture feels by ambiguity, which predicts how much written structure a message must carry: high scorers such as Greece near 100 and Japan near 92 expect detailed agendas, explicit rules and signed detail before acting, while low scorers such as Singapore near 8 and Denmark near 23 will work from an open-ended proposal. It is not risk aversion in the financial sense - a high-scoring culture may take a very large risk, provided the procedure for taking it is spelled out.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how to prepare for a first meeting with a Japanese partner is scored on sending the agenda and documentation in advance rather than planning to improvise.

terms.definition: The specific group a promotional message is designed to reach.
terms.whyItMatters: Defining the audience shapes the message, media, and timing.

terms.definition: A precomputed lookup of billions of password-to-digest pairs that reverses an unprotected stored password in seconds. Adding a distinct random value to each record before hashing defeats it by arithmetic rather than by secrecy: the attacker must now build one table per record, so 1,000,000 stored passwords demand 1,000,000 tables instead of the single shared one.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why one breached company's passwords were readable overnight and another's were not, the competitor has to explain the per-record work multiplier, not just say the second one 'used encryption'.

terms.definition: Total queue wait across all answered contacts divided by the number answered — an arithmetic mean, so it hides the tail. Nine callers waiting 5 seconds and one waiting 300 still reports 34.5 seconds, while the 80/20 service level exposes the outlier because it counts callers rather than averaging them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-improvement roleplay, the competitor who explains why the average looks healthy while customers complain is using this against service level.

terms.definition: A rise in performance produced by a supervisor's high expectations, transmitted through the extra coaching, harder assignments, longer response time and warmer feedback those expectations quietly cause — Rosenthal's finding that the expectation, not the measured ability, moved the outcome. Its negative twin, the Golem effect, does identical damage in the downward direction.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking why two equally skilled new hires diverge under different supervisors expects this, and coaching roleplays are graded on assigning stretch work to the employee the manager privately doubts.

terms.definition: Takes last period's actual as next period's number and nothing else, and exists to be the benchmark: compute its error first, and any model whose MAPE is not meaningfully below that baseline is not paying for the effort it costs, however advanced the technique behind it sounds.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask which forecasting approach a firm should keep; the defensible answer is whichever one beats the zero-effort baseline by a measured margin, and a plan that cannot show that improvement loses the argument for its forecasting spend.

terms.definition: A fixed list of goods and quantities repriced each period; this period's cost divided by the base period's cost, times 100, is the index. A $2,400 basket against a $2,000 base year prints 120, meaning prices are 20% above base — and because the quantities never change, substitution toward cheaper goods is invisible and the index overstates the true rise.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation-impact questions ask a competitor to compute an index from two years of basket costs and then explain why the printed rate overstates what shoppers actually pay.

terms.definition: A brand architecture where one master name fronts every offering and the sub-offerings are descriptors rather than brands — Google Maps, Google Drive, FedEx Freight — so every dollar of marketing on any one product raises awareness for all of them; the opposing structure is a house of brands, where each product owns its equity and one scandal is quarantined to a single name instead of reaching the whole portfolio.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay weighing a launch's branding cost against its risk is decided by naming both architectures and the efficiency-versus-contagion trade between them.

terms.definition: The contract section fixing measurable performance targets and the credit owed when they are missed: 99.9% monthly uptime allows roughly 43 minutes of outage in a 30-day month, and each tier missed below that refunds a stated percentage of the month's fee.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-services roleplays ask what the client is actually promised; converting a percentage into allowed minutes and naming the credit is what makes the promise enforceable.

terms.definition: Completed goal actions divided by the visits or clicks that could have completed them — the denominator is sessions, never impressions — so 40 orders from 2,000 landing-page visits is 2% no matter how many people saw the ad that sent them.
terms.whyItMatters: The single most common analytics error on the marketing exam is dividing sales by impressions; an item that supplies impressions, clicks and orders together is checking which denominator the competitor reaches for.

terms.definition: An independent report on whether a service provider's controls actually operated across an observation window, normally 3 to 12 months of collected evidence. A Type I examines the same controls on one single date and attests only that they were designed correctly — so a vendor holding only a Type I has never had those controls tested over time.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-selection roleplay puts two cloud providers side by side, one with each report; the observation period is the distinction a judge scores.

terms.definition: The actions a business takes to fix a poor experience and restore trust.
terms.whyItMatters: Recovery answers the complaint and negative-feedback scenarios competitors face.

terms.definition: Current assets divided by current liabilities, the standard test of whether a business can cover what it owes within the next twelve months.
terms.whyItMatters: Finance exam items hand over a balance sheet and ask whether the firm can meet short-term obligations; a ratio under 1.0 is the answer that says no.

terms.definition: Catching and sharing another person's feeling state directly instead of inferring it from the outside. It is the branch that reliably triggers helping in the moment, and also the branch that exhausts the helper: compassion fatigue in caregiving and front-line service tracks affective empathy, not the cognitive kind, which is why high-empathy staff burn out faster than indifferent ones.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality and Human Resources roleplays that ask you to coach a front-desk team through a month of hostile guests are scored on whether your plan protects the staff who feel the most, and naming which branch of empathy causes the burnout is what separates a top answer from a sympathetic one.

terms.definition: The number of weeks it takes a campaign's carried-over effect to fall to 50% of its starting level, computed from the weekly retention rate as ln(0.5) ÷ ln(rate) — a rate of 0.7 gives about 1.9 weeks — so a short half-life forces flights roughly monthly while a long one permits long gaps between bursts.
terms.whyItMatters: Flighting-versus-continuity items expect the weeks figure computed, not a description of the trade-off, and the same number sets the measurement window a plan claims when it attributes sales to a campaign.

terms.definition: A product brand that leads with its own name while carrying a visible parent guarantee — Courtyard by Marriott, Polo by Ralph Lauren — sitting between a house of brands, where no parent is shown at all, and a sub-brand, where the parent name leads and the descriptor trails, as in Microsoft Office; the endorsement lends credibility without forcing the parent to own the product's positioning.
terms.whyItMatters: Hotel and hospitality roleplays about launching a new tier are answered with this middle structure, and judges expect the sub-brand contrast to be drawn explicitly.

terms.definition: Scores quality as perception minus expectation on paired 22-item scales across five dimensions -- reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy, responsiveness -- so a dimension scoring 0 means expectations were met exactly and every negative number is a measured shortfall to fix.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how you would measure service quality is scored on the subtraction: measuring satisfaction alone cannot tell an over-promise from an under-delivery.

terms.definition: Government and industry rules governing ad claims, content, and disclosure.
terms.whyItMatters: Compliance protects consumers and shields a business from liability.

terms.definition: The secret-ballot vote that decides union representation: a petition requires authorization cards from at least 30% of the proposed bargaining unit, and certification follows a simple majority of ballots actually cast, not of the unit — 40 votes for out of 70 cast in a 100-person unit certifies the union. A valid election bars another for 12 months, and a resulting contract bars one for up to three years.
terms.whyItMatters: Organizing roleplays test the 30% showing of interest against the majority needed to win, a pair of numbers competitors frequently collapse into one.

terms.definition: Combines two tables and keeps only the rows matching on the join column, silently discarding unmatched rows from both sides — 500 customers joined to an orders table returns nothing at all for the 120 who have never ordered, so a customer count taken after the join reports 380 rather than 500.
terms.whyItMatters: A data-analysis item asks why a mailing list built from a joined query is short by exactly the number of inactive customers; the join type is the entire answer.

terms.definition: Time spent handling contacts and wrap-up divided by time logged in and available — 45 minutes of work inside a 50-minute available hour is 90%. Utilization puts total paid hours in the denominator instead, so it absorbs breaks, training and meetings and always reads lower; sustained occupancy above roughly 85% is the figure that predicts agent burnout.
terms.whyItMatters: A staffing roleplay judged on turnover risk needs the two denominators kept apart, or the schedule looks comfortable on paper and burns the team out.

terms.definition: The self-focused, aversive reaction to witnessing suffering -- an urge for the discomfort to stop that pushes a person to look away, shorten the conversation or avoid the department entirely. Compassion is its other-focused counterpart and moves behavior the opposite way, toward approach and helping; training studies show the two run on different neural systems, so the fix for a withdrawing manager is compassion practice, not more exposure.
terms.whyItMatters: In a Business Law and Ethics Team Decision Making case where a manager keeps avoiding the employee they had to discipline, naming avoidance as distress rather than indifference is what lets you recommend a remedy the judge scores as insight instead of a lecture on caring more.

terms.definition: The distance between the top-down number corporate assumes and the sum of the territory-level bottom-up forecasts, stated as a percentage of the top-down total; a gap past roughly 5% has to be closed by named actions with volume attached to each before the plan is approved, never by splitting the difference.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-approval scenarios hand a corporate target and the field's rolled-up total and expect the gap quantified and assigned; the judge's follow-up is always which specific actions close it and what each is worth.

terms.definition: Groups buyers by what they measurably did — purchase occasion, usage rate, loyalty status, benefit sought — read from transaction records, while psychographic segmentation groups them by what they say they value and geographic segmentation by where they live; a heavy user and a light user can match on every demographic and psychographic trait and still belong in different behavioral segments, so it is the only base that predicts volume directly.
terms.whyItMatters: Loyalty-program roleplays ask which customers to reward; the winning answer segments on measured usage rate rather than on who the customers are.

terms.definition: Planning, executing, and monitoring work to hit objectives within time and budget.
terms.whyItMatters: It lets managers coordinate resources and deliver on schedule.

terms.definition: Sells the finished product with its full marketing plan in a few representative cities while matched control cities keep the old plan, so the result read is the difference between the two areas rather than the test area's raw sales; the cost is secrecy, since rivals see the plan months early.
terms.whyItMatters: Launch roleplays ask how you would prove the plan works before national rollout; the matched control is the detail that turns a demo into a measurement.

terms.definition: A purchase credited to an ad that was served and seen but never clicked, counted only when it falls inside a fixed look-back window — commonly one day for display against 30 days for a click — which is why these totals overstate a campaign next to click-through conversions.
terms.whyItMatters: A results presentation where the platform's reported sales exceed the client's actual order count is this in action, and the competitor is expected to say which conversions were assumed rather than observed.

terms.definition: A state privacy law binding a for-profit business only once it crosses one of three thresholds: more than $25 million in annual gross revenue, personal information on 100,000 or more California consumers or households, or at least 50% of revenue earned from selling or sharing that information. A small firm holding California data can sit entirely outside it.
terms.whyItMatters: A legal-issues item asks whether a startup with 4,000 California customers and $2 million in revenue must honor deletion requests; only the thresholds answer it.

terms.definition: The share of paid staff time not available to take contacts — breaks, training, meetings, absence and paid leave. A center budgeting 30% shrinkage must schedule about 1.43 bodies for every agent it needs live on the phones, because 1 divided by 0.70 is 1.43; ignoring it understaffs a peak by roughly a third.
terms.whyItMatters: Peaks-in-demand roleplays ask how many people to put on the schedule, and the gross-up is where the answer is won or lost.

terms.definition: The measured loss of an activity's intrinsic appeal after an expected external reward is introduced and later withdrawn — the person rereads their own reason for acting as having done it for the payment. Rewards that arrive unexpectedly, or that carry information about competence rather than control, do not produce the same crowding out, which is why a surprise thank-you outperforms a standing bounty.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing an incentive for a task employees already enjoy is scored on anticipating this backfire, and exam items on recognizing contributions reward unexpected, informational recognition.

terms.definition: Duty a broker-dealer owes to recommend products that fit a customer's stated objectives, raised in 2020 to a best-interest obligation requiring conflicts to be disclosed. It still stops short of the fiduciary standard a registered investment adviser owes under the Advisers Act of 1940, where the client's interest comes first continuously, not only at the moment of a recommendation.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-advising roleplay about recommending a higher-commission fund turns on which of the two duties the professional is actually held to.

terms.definition: The spending level on a diminishing-returns response curve where the last dollar invested returns exactly one dollar of contribution; below it more spending still adds profit, above it volume keeps climbing while profit falls, so the stopping test is marginal contribution per marginal dollar equal to 1.0 — not whether total return is still positive.
terms.whyItMatters: Budget items deliberately show total return positive at every spending level to see whether the competitor stops at the marginal break-even; a plan arguing for more spend past that point is refuted with its own numbers.

terms.definition: Launching into a different product category under an existing brand name — Dove soap into Dove shampoo — whereas a line extension adds a variant inside the category the brand already sells, such as another Dove soap scent; the category jump risks diluting what the parent name means, while the in-category variant mainly risks stealing volume from its own siblings, so the two carry different failure modes and different tests.
terms.whyItMatters: Product roleplays that hand you a growth mandate are scored on naming which of the two you chose and the specific risk it carries; treating them as the same move loses both points.

terms.definition: Locates a failure in one of five gaps -- not knowing what customers expect, setting wrong standards, delivery that misses those standards, promotion promising what operations cannot deliver, and the customer gap between expectation and perception, which is produced by the first four.
terms.whyItMatters: Guest-recovery roleplays are scored on diagnosing which gap caused the complaint, since an over-promising ad and an untrained server call for opposite fixes.

terms.definition: A schedule that alternates concentrated bursts with hiatus periods carrying no advertising at all — eight weeks on, four weeks dark — which buys higher in-season frequency than a flat continuous weight, at the cost of awareness decay during the dark weeks.
terms.whyItMatters: Seasonal-business roleplays turn on choosing this over pulsing or continuity, and the competitor is expected to name the trade the client is making rather than simply calling the plan seasonal.

terms.definition: The legally fixed span between learning of a personal-data breach and having to report it — 72 hours to the supervising authority under EU rules, with U.S. state statutes commonly allowing 30 to 60 days for notice to the individuals affected. The clock starts at awareness, not at the intrusion, so an attack that sat undetected for 8 months still leaves the full window intact once it is found.
terms.whyItMatters: An incident roleplay asks when the company is late; competitors who count from the intrusion date report the firm as months overdue when it is in fact on day one.

terms.definition: The slow divergence between a firm's strategy and its changing environment as incremental adjustments preserve old assumptions, ending in a flux period and either transformational change or failure; the danger is that performance looks fine while the gap widens.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about a long-successful retailer losing ground to online rivals are scored on diagnosing the widening environment gap rather than blaming a single bad quarter.

terms.definition: Adjusting communication and approach to cultural and social differences.
terms.whyItMatters: Culturally aware service builds stronger, more diverse relationships.

terms.definition: A trait-level difficulty identifying and describing one's own feelings, paired with an externally oriented thinking style; measured on the 20-item Toronto scale and present in roughly one in ten adults. It is not suppression and not coldness -- the states are experienced physically, as fatigue or a knotted stomach, and simply cannot be named, so telling such a person to open up produces a description of events rather than of feeling.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core items on assessing personal strengths test whether you know that a teammate who reports nothing when asked how a project felt may be unable to name it rather than unwilling; the Human Resources roleplay remedy is a written checklist of options, not more probing questions.

terms.definition: The percentage volume increase a discount must produce merely to hold contribution flat: discount per unit ÷ (normal contribution per unit − discount per unit). A $1 cut against $4 of unit contribution needs 33% more units; a $2 cut against the same $4 needs 100%, which is why deep cuts almost never pay for themselves.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion-approval questions give margin and discount depth and expect the required lift computed and compared with the forecast lift; anything forecast below the break-even figure is a promotion the plan should reject.

terms.definition: Share of respondents who name a brand when asked only to list the brands they can think of in a category with nothing shown to them, as opposed to aided awareness, where the interviewer reads the name and the respondent only confirms recognition; aided scores typically run two to four times higher than unaided ones, so the two measures can never be compared with each other or with a competitor's differently-worded question.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays that hand you awareness research want you to challenge the number's basis before acting on it; treating an aided figure as proof of strong awareness is the standard trap.

terms.definition: Something buyers do not think to look for and may not know exists, so it has to be sold to them rather than bought -- burial plots, life insurance, a brand-new category's first entrant; a specialty good is the opposite pole, actively hunted by name with special effort.
terms.whyItMatters: Selling roleplays for insurance or services are scored on recognizing that no one walks in asking, which forces prospecting and personal selling rather than displays.

terms.definition: Discretionary money a vendor awards a partner for a pre-approved marketing plan and pays only on proof of performance, with no entitlement based on past volume. Co-op funds work the opposite way: they accrue AUTOMATICALLY as a stated percentage of what the partner already purchased, so co-op rewards history while MDF buys a specific future activity, often from partners too new to have accrued anything.
terms.whyItMatters: Coordinating channel work with promotion is a tested indicator, and roleplays ask how to fund a new partner's launch when there is no purchase history to accrue against.

terms.definition: A randomly selected slice of the target deliberately shown no advertising, so campaign lift is the exposed group's conversion rate minus the withheld group's — if exposed converts at 3.2% and the holdout at 2.6%, only 0.6 points were caused by the campaign and the rest would have happened anyway.
terms.whyItMatters: A client convinced a campaign drove every sale in its window is the setup for this method, and a competitor who can propose withholding a control group is answering a measurement question that platform-reported totals cannot.

terms.definition: Pairs every row of one table with every row of another under no condition at all, so the output is m × n rows — 50 products against 12 months yields 600. A two-table query whose join condition is left off collapses into one, which is how a query over 1,000 and 2,000 rows returns 2,000,000 and freezes the report.
terms.whyItMatters: A troubleshooting item shows a report that suddenly returns millions of rows from two small tables; the multiplication, not the data, explains it.

terms.definition: A queuing formula that converts contact volume, average handle time and a target answer speed into required agents, and its output is non-linear: doubling volume needs well under double the staff, while removing the last agent from a tight schedule can multiply wait time. Averages alone cannot produce the answer because arrivals are random, not evenly spaced.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains the counter-intuitive result in a staffing case — cutting one agent from a 20-agent schedule can break an 80/20 target outright.

terms.definition: The claim that self-control draws on one limited resource that earlier exertion uses up. The original effects were large, but a 2016 multi-lab registered replication with over 2,000 participants found the effect near zero, and the defensible version now is motivational: people who believe willpower is limited show the drop-off and people who do not, largely do not. Citing the fuel-tank version as settled fact is the error.
terms.whyItMatters: Stress-management questions on the Business Administration Core exam still offer 'willpower runs out' as a distractor; knowing the replication result is what keeps you from choosing it, and from building a roleplay schedule recommendation on a decision-fatigue premise a judge with a psychology background will not accept.

terms.definition: Period sales divided by that period's seasonal index — 130,000 units in a month carrying an index of 1.30 is 100,000 on a level basis — and any trend line must be fitted to these adjusted figures, because fitting a line straight to raw seasonal data reads the busy season as growth that is not there.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast items hand monthly actuals alongside indexes and expect the adjusted series produced before any projection; skipping the division is the standard error that inflates a plan's growth claim and gets caught on the follow-up.

terms.definition: Gap between two group means divided by their pooled standard deviation, so 0.2 reads as small, 0.5 as medium and 0.8 as large; it answers how big the difference is, where a significance test only answers whether it is likely real. With 50,000 respondents a d of 0.05 can clear p less than 0.05 and still be worth nothing commercially.
terms.whyItMatters: Turning findings into a recommendation means saying whether a difference is large enough to act on, and this is the number that separates a meaningful gap from a merely detectable one.

terms.definition: Lost unit sales of a firm's existing products divided by the unit sales of the new product that displaced them — 30,000 new units alongside a 12,000-unit drop on the old line is a 40% rate, leaving 18,000 units of true incremental volume; a launch reported on gross volume alone can show growth while total company units fall, which is why the ratio is computed before the launch is called a success.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay presenting strong launch numbers usually hides this; asking for the effect on the existing line is what separates a scored answer from applause.

terms.definition: The band between desired service, what the customer hopes for, and adequate service, the least they will accept: performance inside the band passes unnoticed, above it delights, below it triggers complaint or defection, and the band narrows sharply in urgent or first-time-fix situations.
