terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about exceeding guest expectations are scored on knowing that ordinary delivery earns nothing; the band explains why effort spent in the middle is invisible.

terms.definition: Google Ads' 1-to-10 diagnostic combining expected clickthrough rate, ad relevance and landing-page experience; it multiplies into the bid to set ad position, so an advertiser bidding $2.00 with a score of 8 outranks one bidding $3.00 with a score of 4 and pays less per click.
terms.whyItMatters: A search-advertising roleplay where the client wants to win position by raising the bid is the classic misread; the cheaper fix is tightening ad-to-keyword-to-page relevance, and the exam tests all three components by name.

terms.definition: The 128-bit addressing scheme succeeding the 32-bit scheme the internet was built on. Because each added bit doubles the space, 128 bits is not four times larger but 2^96 times larger — the older scheme's roughly 4.3 billion addresses ran out, and the newer one is written as eight hexadecimal groups rather than four decimal ones.
terms.whyItMatters: An item on the scope of the internet asks why address exhaustion forced a change instead of an expansion; the doubling, not the label, is the explanation.

terms.definition: Fully loaded center cost — wages, benefits, technology and facilities — divided by contacts handled; $180,000 a month across 30,000 contacts is $6.00 each. A live phone contact typically runs several times the cost of a self-service session, and that spread, not the software licence, is the business case for deflection.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay proposing a chatbot or a help center has to set this figure against the deflected channel to justify the spend.

terms.definition: Consistently low prices instead of frequent sales or promotions.
terms.whyItMatters: EDLP offers a sustainable cost-leadership pricing approach.

terms.definition: The precision with which a person tells their own states apart -- 'slighted', 'apprehensive' and 'resentful' rather than one undifferentiated 'bad'. It is not vocabulary for its own sake: people high in it need fewer and less extreme regulation strategies, retaliate less when provoked in lab aggression tasks, and drink less to cope, so the act of discriminating the state does regulatory work by itself.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core exam items on self-assessment reward the competitor who can say what specifically went wrong in a conflict; a roleplay answer that reports feeling 'stressed' scores below one that separates being overloaded from being undermined, because the two call for different actions.

terms.definition: Divides a town's retail sales per resident by the state's retail sales per resident: 1.00 means locals spend exactly the statewide average at home, above 1.00 means the town is pulling shoppers in from outside its borders, and 0.80 means a fifth of local buying power is leaking to other towns.
terms.whyItMatters: Trading-area and site questions give local and statewide sales per person and expect the ratio plus a read on leakage; it is the figure behind arguing that a market is under-served and can support another store.

terms.definition: Plots competing brands against two axes chosen from the attributes buyers actually use to tell brands apart — often price against perceived quality — using respondent ratings rather than the firm's own specifications, and adds an ideal point where the target segment says it wants a brand to sit; an empty region on the map is a positioning opportunity only when an ideal point falls inside it, otherwise it is empty because nobody wants that combination.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning roleplays that hand you competitor data are scored on naming the two axes and defending why buyers discriminate on them; competitors lose the point by mapping attributes only the company cares about.

terms.definition: A tangible item expected to survive repeated use, the standard statistical cutoff being an expected life of three years or more, which is why appliances and vehicles qualify; nondurables are consumed in one or a few uses and are bought on habit rather than deliberation.
terms.whyItMatters: Warranty, financing, and personal-selling effort all follow this split, so an exam item on why one product gets a service plan and another does not is answered with the three-year line.

terms.definition: Total spend divided by clicks received — $800 over 3,200 clicks is $0.25 — a pricing basis that charges only when someone acts, unlike cost per thousand, which charges for the impression whether or not anyone ever clicks it.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-promotion roleplay asks which pricing model protects a small client's budget; the answer turns on whether the goal is awareness, where impressions are the product, or traffic, where only the click is worth paying for.

terms.definition: One deal's single commission pool divided between the rep who sourced it and the rep who closed it — 50/50, 30/70 or whatever the plan states — and the shares must total 100 percent. It changes who gets paid, never how much the company pays out, which is exactly the point students miss when they assume both reps earn a full commission.
terms.whyItMatters: Compensation items give a deal value, a commission rate and two named reps and check whether you double the payout; a team-selling roleplay expects you to settle credit before the sale, not after.

terms.definition: A 32-bit pattern splitting an address into a network part and a host part: a /24 leaves 8 bits for hosts, which is 2^8 = 256 addresses, of which 254 are assignable once the network and broadcast addresses come out. A /25 halves that to 126 usable, so borrowing a single bit costs half the room on the segment.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how many devices a store's network segment can hold, the competitor must convert the slash number into host bits and then subtract 2 — the raw power of two is the wrong answer.

terms.definition: Systems and strategies for managing customer data, interactions, and relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: CRM tracks preferences and delivers personalized service at scale.

terms.definition: Arousal and performance trace an inverted U rather than a straight line, and the peak moves with task difficulty: simple, well-practiced work peaks at high arousal, while complex or unfamiliar work peaks at markedly lower arousal. The practical consequence is counterintuitive -- getting keyed up helps most on the easy task and hurts most on the hard one, so pep talks are misapplied precisely where the stakes are highest.
terms.whyItMatters: Presenting a rehearsed 60-second close benefits from adrenaline; solving an unfamiliar Team Decision Making case in the prep room does not, and exam items on stress management test whether you can pick the right side of that curve for a named task.

terms.definition: Compares an industry's share of local employment or sales with its share nationally — local share ÷ national share — so 1.0 marks a perfectly typical market, above about 1.25 says the activity is concentrated here and likely serves customers beyond it, and below about 0.75 says local demand is being met from somewhere else.
terms.whyItMatters: Situation-analysis questions supply local and national employment figures and expect the ratio read against 1.0; it is how a plan defends choosing one metro over another with evidence rather than preference.

terms.definition: Two independently known brands appear together on one finished offering and both stake positioning risk on it — a Doritos Locos Taco — whereas in ingredient branding one brand is a component inside a host product and is advertised to end users to pull the host's sales, as with Intel Inside; the ingredient brand never owns the final purchase decision, while co-brands share it and share the damage if the partner stumbles.
terms.whyItMatters: Partnership roleplays ask what each side actually contributes and risks; naming which of the two structures is on the table is the first thing the judge listens for.

terms.definition: Bars earlier or contemporaneous statements, oral or written, that would contradict a writing the parties intended as their complete and final agreement — a merger or integration clause is the usual signal of that intent. Evidence of fraud, duress, ambiguity, an unsatisfied condition precedent, or a later modification still comes in, because the rule blocks contradiction of the past and never blocks changes made afterward.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a customer insists the salesperson promised free installation that appears nowhere in the signed order turns on this rule and its fraud exception.

terms.definition: The severest federal recall classification, used when a defect carries a reasonable probability of serious injury or death; Class II covers defects whose harm is temporary or medically reversible and where serious harm is remote, and Class III covers violations unlikely to cause any harm.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-protection questions give a defect scenario and ask how urgently the firm must act; the class decides the notification reach and the speed regulators expect.

terms.definition: Opens divided by messages delivered — not messages sent — so 4,000 opens on 20,000 delivered is 20% while the same 4,000 against 25,000 sent looks like 16%. The count only fires when a tracking pixel loads, so image blocking and Apple's Mail Privacy Protection both distort it.
terms.whyItMatters: A direct-marketing roleplay reporting a suspiciously high figure after a privacy change is testing whether the competitor knows the metric is inferred from a pixel and will point to clicks as the reliable measure instead.

terms.definition: Hits divided by total lookups — 900 of 1,000 is 90%. Read as percentage points the figure misleads: moving from 90% to 95% cuts the 100 misses that reach the database down to 50, so a five-point gain halves backend load, and the last few points are worth far more than the first.
terms.whyItMatters: A technology-impact item asks whether a small improvement to a caching layer is worth the spend; the answer runs on misses removed, not on the headline percentage.

terms.definition: Closed cases a customer reopens divided by cases closed in the period — 60 of 1,200 is 5%. It is the audit on first contact resolution: an agent can inflate the resolution figure by closing tickets early, and this is the only metric that catches it, which is why the two are always reported as a pair.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-quality case, the competitor who pairs a resolution claim with this check shows the judge they know the headline metric can be gamed.

terms.definition: Putting a feeling into words as an implicit regulation move. Naming the state lowers amygdala response and self-reported intensity, yet people asked in advance predict the opposite -- that saying it out loud will make it worse -- which is why the technique is deliberately taught and does not get used spontaneously. It is not venting, which rehearses the emotion at length and tends to raise arousal instead.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay judge plays an escalating customer or a blindsided direct report, opening by naming the other person's state out loud is a scoreable de-escalation move; competitors who default to defending the policy first talk into a rising emotion.

terms.definition: Sorts national communication styles into three categories rather than scoring dimensions: linear-active cultures (Germany, Switzerland, the U.S.) plan sequentially, do one thing at a time and argue from facts; multi-active cultures (Italy, Brazil, much of Africa) speak over one another, run several tasks at once and put the relationship ahead of the schedule; reactive cultures (Japan, China, Finland) listen first, do not interrupt, and answer only after a silence that outsiders misread as disagreement. Each country lands in one category, which is what makes it usable mid-meeting where a six-dimension score is not.
terms.whyItMatters: An international roleplay in which the counterpart falls silent after your proposal is scored on reading the pause as a reactive-style norm instead of filling it with an unnecessary concession.

terms.definition: The overall approach a business uses to reach customers and meet marketing goals.
terms.whyItMatters: Case studies require strategies that fit business objectives and market conditions.

terms.definition: Weakening of a famous mark's distinctiveness through blurring, where an unrelated use erodes the one-to-one link between mark and source, or tarnishment, where a use ties it to something unsavory; under the U.S. Trademark Dilution Revision Act of 2006 the owner of a mark famous to the general consuming public can sue without showing any likelihood of confusion or proof of actual economic injury, which is what makes it broader than ordinary infringement.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding and business-law roleplays about a licensing or extension request turn on this doctrine; citing the no-confusion-required standard is the technical half of the answer.

terms.definition: The Consumer Product Safety Act duty to notify the Commission within 24 hours of obtaining information that a product contains a defect creating a substantial hazard, fails a mandatory standard, or poses an unreasonable risk -- and the duty applies even when the firm still disputes the defect.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics and consumer-protection roleplays test whether you report before finishing your own investigation; waiting for certainty is the answer that loses the indicator and, in practice, draws the fine.

terms.definition: Copies a publication actually distributes in an average issue, audited by the Alliance for Audited Media, as opposed to readership, which multiplies those copies by a pass-along factor of roughly 2 to 3 — so a 500,000-copy magazine can legitimately claim 1,200,000 readers.
terms.whyItMatters: Print-buying items give one vehicle's audited copies and a rival's claimed readers and ask which is the larger audience; the competitor has to convert both to the same basis before the cost-per-thousand comparison means anything.

terms.definition: The 1,024-based unit an operating system counts in, set against the 1,000-based unit a drive is sold in: a '1 TB' disk holds 10^12 bytes, but the OS divides by 1,024 three times and reports 931 GB — a 7% shortfall that widens at every prefix step, so a 4 TB drive shows as 3.64 TB, roughly 9% short.
terms.whyItMatters: A records-storage item asks how many years of files a purchased drive really holds; sizing the archive off the number on the box overstates capacity before the first backup runs.

terms.definition: The forward premium on a currency has to equal the gap between the two countries' interest rates, or borrowing in one and lending in the other earns a riskless profit. A 5% domestic rate against 2% abroad implies the foreign currency trades forward about 3% above spot, which cancels the yield advantage exactly.
terms.whyItMatters: International-finance items ask why a competitor should not simply park cash in the highest-yielding currency; the forward discount is the answer.

terms.definition: The clock from a customer's message to the first substantive human reply, which stops on that reply even though nothing is fixed yet; resolution time runs on until the issue is actually closed. A 1-hour response with a 3-day resolution is a legitimate and common pair, and quoting one figure for both makes a team look twice as fast as it is.
terms.whyItMatters: Email and social-service roleplays set two separate targets, so a competitor who reports a single number has misread the case.

terms.definition: Within the transactional model of stress, the same demand is coded as a challenge when perceived resources meet or exceed it and as a threat when they fall short. The two states are physiologically opposite -- challenge raises cardiac output while blood vessels dilate, threat constricts them -- and challenge predicts better performance under identical objective pressure, so the leverage point is the resource estimate, not the demand.
terms.whyItMatters: Coaching a nervous teammate before a Team Decision Making presentation works by listing what the team already has, not by insisting the case is easy; exam items on stress management reward the answer that changes the appraisal rather than the workload.

terms.definition: The ceiling on category demand in a defined area and period — every possible buyer times the maximum quantity each could buy times unit price; one firm's share of that ceiling is sales potential, and the volume it actually expects to sell on the funded budget is the sales forecast.
terms.whyItMatters: Sizing items on the marketing exam hand you a population, a purchase rate and a price and expect the whole-industry ceiling, not one company's number; in a market-identification roleplay the judge is listening for the three-step narrowing said in order.

terms.definition: A one-sentence internal formula built from four required elements — the target segment, the frame of reference (the category the brand is to be compared against), the point of difference, and the reason to believe that substantiates it; drop the frame of reference and the claim has no competitive set to be better than, drop the reason to believe and it is an assertion. It is never customer-facing copy, which is the tagline's job.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges frequently ask a competitor to state the positioning out loud; delivering all four elements in one sentence is the difference between a scored answer and a slogan.

terms.definition: Nothing can be inspected, weighed, or returned before purchase, so buyers judge search qualities beforehand, experience qualities only during delivery, and credence qualities -- a surgeon's technique, a tax opinion -- never at all; a good lets buyers verify most attributes before paying.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay contrasting service marketing with product marketing is scored on the tangible cues you add -- uniforms, facilities, guarantees -- to stand in for inspection.

terms.definition: Current assets minus inventory, divided by current liabilities — the stricter liquidity test, because inventory may not convert to cash in time to pay a bill.
terms.whyItMatters: A retailer with a healthy current ratio and a weak quick ratio is the classic exam case, and the difference is inventory the business cannot sell fast.

terms.definition: An email permanently rejected because the address does not exist or the domain is dead, as opposed to a soft bounce, which is a temporary failure such as a full mailbox or a server outage and gets retried; mailbox providers begin filtering a sender whose permanent-failure rate passes roughly 2%.
terms.whyItMatters: A client whose newsletter suddenly lands in spam usually has an unpurged list, and a direct-marketing roleplay expects the competitor to distinguish the two failure types before recommending list hygiene.

terms.definition: A spreadsheet address locking exactly one of the two coordinates — $B5 pins the column and lets the row travel, B$5 does the reverse. Filling a multiplication grid both across and down needs one of each inside the same formula ($B5*C$4); pinning both coordinates or neither returns a wrong value in every cell except the one it was typed into.
terms.whyItMatters: Spreadsheet items grade the filled grid rather than the first cell, so a formula that is correct where it is written and wrong everywhere it is dragged scores zero.

terms.definition: Contacts passed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier divided by total contacts. A transfer moves a contact sideways to a peer queue; an escalation moves it up a level of authority — so an agent whose refund limit is $50 must escalate every $60 refund, and the rate is measuring the policy, not the customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about empowering frontline staff turn on this: raising an agent's approval limit is usually the cheapest way to cut it.

terms.definition: Passivity that persists after control returns, following exposure to events the person could not control. The 2016 reversal by the original researchers matters more than the classic story: passivity turns out to be the unlearned default under prolonged bad events, and what is actually acquired is the detection of control. The opposite style is scored on three axes -- whether a setback is read as permanent, as pervasive across life, and as personal.
terms.whyItMatters: A Human Resources roleplay about a team that stopped submitting ideas after two years of vetoes is solved by restoring a visible, controllable decision, not by a motivation speech -- and Business Administration Core items on maintaining a positive attitude test the three-axis explanation, not vague optimism.

terms.definition: Discovering and defining the markets where a business can sell its offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Identifying the right market is the foundation of any marketing plan.

terms.definition: A rating form whose points are each defined by a real example of observable behavior — a 5 might read greets every guest within thirty seconds while a 2 reads acknowledges guests only after they approach — built from critical incidents gathered from people who do the job. A plain graphic rating scale labels the same points only excellent through poor, which is why two managers can rate identical behavior differently on it.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay complains that appraisals are inconsistent between supervisors, the tested fix is anchoring each scale point in described behavior.

terms.definition: Values a brand as the licensing fee the owner avoids paying by owning it: forecast the revenue the brand will carry, multiply by an arm's-length royalty rate drawn from comparable licenses — commonly 2% to 6% of net sales — deduct tax, then discount the resulting stream to present value; unlike a cost-based valuation it ignores what was actually spent building the name, and unlike a market comparison it needs no sale of a similar brand.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking what the brand is worth on the balance sheet expects a named valuation method with its arithmetic, not the claim that a brand cannot be valued.

terms.definition: A label a written warranty may carry only if it repairs defects free within a reasonable time, puts no duty on the buyer beyond giving notice, does not limit the duration of implied warranties, and offers a refund or replacement after a reasonable number of failed repairs; missing any one forces the 'limited' label.
terms.whyItMatters: Warranty roleplays ask what a store may print on the tag; a written warranty that charges a handling fee cannot be called full, and knowing which of the four conditions broke is the scoring point.

terms.definition: A medium's published open prices per unit of time or space, quoted before any negotiation; national buyers routinely settle 30% to 50% under them, so a media plan costed at these published figures overstates what the buy will actually cost.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a small client is handed a station's published prices tests whether the competitor knows the quoted number is an opening position, and a plan built on it will look unaffordable when it is not.

terms.definition: Raw, unprocessed facts and figures collected through observation, measurement, or research.
terms.whyItMatters: All information management begins with knowing what counts as reliable data.

terms.definition: Help-center or bot sessions that end without a human contact, divided by total sessions — 7,000 of 10,000 is 70%. A session only counts as deflected when no contact follows inside a set window, usually 24 hours; without that window an abandoned bot session where the customer gave up and phoned later is scored as a save.
terms.whyItMatters: The savings claim in a technology-in-CRM roleplay collapses without the follow-up window, and judges look for the competitor who states it.

terms.definition: Average daily usage multiplied by lead time in days, plus safety stock — the on-hand level that triggers a replenishment order, so it answers WHEN to order while economic order quantity answers HOW MUCH.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give you daily usage, a supplier lead time and a buffer and ask at what stock level a buyer should place the reorder; picking the order size instead of the trigger level is the standard wrong answer.

terms.definition: A systematic failure to predict how a different visceral state will drive behavior. The gap runs within one person across states, not between two people: the same competitor, calm, underestimates what anger, hunger, fear or a ticking clock will make them concede, and having previously been in the hot state does not repair the forecast. It is why rules set in advance beat intentions set in advance.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors rehearse a price floor calmly and then give away margin under a hostile buyer in the ten minutes of a Marketing or Business Services roleplay; writing the walk-away number down before the prep clock starts is the countermeasure this concept prescribes.

terms.definition: One company's maximum obtainable slice of category demand — market potential multiplied by the highest share it could hold with unlimited marketing effort; it always sits above the sales forecast, which discounts that ceiling down to the effort and budget actually approved.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that give an industry ceiling and a best-case share expect this middle figure, and a competitor who reports it as the forecast overstates the plan's revenue line in front of a judge.

terms.definition: Three decisions taken strictly in order — segment the market on one chosen base, target the segments worth serving against a stated attractiveness test, then position the offer against a named competitive set — where each step's output constrains the next; a positioning claim written before the segment is chosen has nobody in particular to be different for, which is why reordering the letters produces a plan that cannot be defended.
terms.whyItMatters: Marketing-plan roleplays are graded on sequence as much as content; presenting a promotion idea before naming the segment invites the judge to ask who it is for.

terms.definition: Production and consumption happen at the same instant with the buyer present, so the employee is part of the product and no defective unit can be caught before a customer receives it; a manufactured good is built, inspected, and warehoused weeks before anyone buys it.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-quality roleplays are scored on front-line hiring and training as quality control, because there is no inspection step to add between production and the customer.

terms.definition: The 2003 federal statute governing commercial email: every message needs truthful headers and subject line, a valid physical postal address, and an opt-out mechanism honored within 10 business days, with civil penalties assessed per individual message sent rather than per campaign.
terms.whyItMatters: An email-promotion roleplay where a client wants to keep mailing customers who unsubscribed is a compliance question with a specific deadline attached, and the per-message penalty structure is what makes a single bad send expensive.

terms.definition: Statement of the principles a profession owes the public, enforced by a licensing or membership board that can suspend or revoke the credential itself. A code of conduct is narrower and employer-issued: it lists prohibited acts and is enforced through progressive discipline up to termination, which ends the job but leaves the right to practice intact.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where an employee follows company policy yet violates a professional standard requires naming which body can act and what each can take away.

terms.definition: Reached only when a table already satisfies first normal form, which removes repeating groups so each cell holds one value, and second normal form, which removes any non-key column depending on just part of a composite key, and then additionally removes transitive dependency — a non-key column determined by another non-key column rather than by the key.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam table showing a customer's ZIP code alongside the city that ZIP code determines is the classic normalization item, and the tested answer names which form that violation breaks.

terms.definition: A grid that derives a case's priority from how many people or how much revenue is affected, set against how fast the situation degrades — high impact with high urgency becomes P1, high impact with low urgency P2, and so on across a 3x3 or 4x4 grid. Priority is computed from the two axes rather than argued by whoever complains loudest.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a backlog of angry customers in a roleplay, the competitor who sorts by this grid instead of by volume of complaint wins the judged point on fairness.

terms.definition: Passive, self-critical dwelling on the causes of a bad feeling -- 'why do I always'. Splitting self-focused thought into brooding and reflective pondering is the point: only the brooding component predicts later depressive symptoms, while reflection is neutral or mildly protective. So 'thinking it over' is two different behaviors with opposite outcomes, and the sortable difference is whether the thought is aimed at a cause or at a next action.
terms.whyItMatters: Feedback-handling items on the Business Administration Core exam and roleplays that ask you to debrief a lost account both reward turning a replay of the failure into one named change; a competitor who describes going over it again and again is describing the harmful half.

terms.definition: Sizing demand from the bottom up: identify every potential buyer in each segment or territory, estimate units each would buy, and sum units times price across them. The chain-ratio method runs the opposite direction, starting from a national total and multiplying it down through successive percentages.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business sizing cases on the exam name a count of establishments and a per-establishment purchase rate, which is a buildup problem; using a national percentage chain there produces the wrong answer.

terms.definition: The overall look and feel of a product or its packaging — the contour of a Coca-Cola bottle, a restaurant chain's interior scheme — protected under Lanham Act section 43(a) only when it is non-functional and has acquired secondary meaning in buyers' minds; product design trade dress can never be inherently distinctive, so unlike a coined word mark it always requires evidence that consumers link the look to a single source.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about a competitor copying a store's look are scored on naming this protection and its two conditions; calling it a trademark or a copyright is the common miss.

terms.definition: Raising follower motivation through vision, individualized attention, and intellectual stimulation so people exceed the stated requirement; transactional leadership instead trades contingent reward for compliance and corrects by exception, which sustains performance but rarely changes it.
terms.whyItMatters: Leadership roleplays that ask how to re-energize a team after a merger reward the transformational levers by name, with the transactional contrast used to explain why bonuses alone stalled.

terms.definition: The liability booked at the moment of sale for repairs expected later -- units sold times expected claim rate times cost per claim, so 100,000 units at a 2% claim rate and $40 per claim accrues $80,000 of expense in the period the revenue is recognized, not when the repairs happen.
terms.whyItMatters: Questions pairing a generous warranty with its cost are answered with this accrual; a roleplay proposing a longer warranty has to price it, and the reserve is the number to quote.

terms.definition: Replacement time or space a medium owes when a commitment ran in the wrong position, ran late, or fell short of guaranteed delivery — a station that guarantees 150 gross rating points and delivers 120 owes those 30 points back as inventory, not as a cash refund.
terms.whyItMatters: An under-delivery roleplay tests whether the competitor asks for the right remedy; demanding money back where the contract promises replacement inventory usually forfeits the claim entirely.

terms.definition: An organized, computer-managed collection of related data that can be stored and retrieved systematically.
terms.whyItMatters: Businesses run everything from inventory to customer records on databases.

terms.definition: A total outage or safety-affecting failure with no workaround, carrying the tightest published clock — commonly a 15-minute acknowledgement, hourly status updates and continuous work until restoration. Severity rates the technical damage while priority adds business context, so a Sev-1 affecting one tiny account can still be worked at P2.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-level roleplays hinge on the severity-versus-priority split, and quoting the acknowledgement clock is what makes the answer specific rather than reassuring.

terms.definition: The proposed tipping point of positive to negative interactions above which a team or relationship flourishes, popularized as a precise 2.9013 to 1. The exact figure was withdrawn in 2013 after the nonlinear-dynamics mathematics behind it was shown to be invalid, leaving a real but coarse finding: more positive than negative helps, and the specific number does not survive scrutiny. Quoting the decimal as science is the trap.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges hear the tidy ratio in motivation and team-climate roleplays every year; recommending a deliberate surplus of recognition over correction while declining to name a magic number is the answer that holds up if a judge asks where the figure comes from.

terms.definition: The path a product takes from producer or provider to the final customer.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel choices affect convenience, cost, access, and customer experience.

terms.definition: The specific customer group a business chooses as its primary marketing audience.
terms.whyItMatters: Recommendations are stronger when they name a specific audience.

terms.definition: Incremental gross profit from a campaign minus its marketing cost, divided by that marketing cost: $150,000 of incremental revenue at a 40% gross margin against $30,000 of spend is ($60,000 - $30,000) / $30,000, or 100%. It runs on margin rather than revenue, and only on the lift a holdout group shows the campaign actually caused, so a campaign whose sales would have happened anyway returns a negative figure no matter how large the revenue number looks.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks whether a promotion paid for itself, the graded answer is this ratio on margin with a baseline, not the raw sales the campaign period produced.

terms.definition: Unused capacity is destroyed the moment it goes unsold: a 200-room hotel that sells 150 rooms tonight cannot add the other 50 to tomorrow's inventory, which is why capacity is priced by demand period; unsold physical goods simply stay in inventory and sell later.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about slow midweek nights are scored on demand-shifting tactics -- off-peak pricing, overbooking policy -- that follow directly from capacity that cannot be stored.

terms.definition: The FTC doctrine that an advertiser must already hold the evidence for an objective claim before that claim runs, and that health or performance claims require competent and reliable scientific evidence — the line separating a provable assertion from puffery, which makes no measurable claim and needs no proof.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay client who wants to advertise that a product works twice as fast is asking a legal question, and the competitor is scored on requiring the proof up front rather than promising to find it if challenged.

terms.definition: The four guarantees a relational transaction makes — atomicity, meaning all steps commit or none do; consistency, meaning no declared rule is left broken; isolation, meaning concurrent transactions cannot read each other's partial work; and durability, meaning a committed write survives a crash — and precisely the set that BASE-style distributed stores relax in exchange for availability.
terms.whyItMatters: A banking-transfer scenario asks what keeps a debit from posting when the matching credit fails, and the graded answer names atomicity within this set rather than saying the system is careful.

terms.definition: Square of the correlation coefficient, read as the share of variation in the outcome that the model accounts for: r of 0.60 gives 0.36, so 36 percent is explained and 64 percent is left to everything else. It is not the slope, and a high value still proves association rather than causation.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a regression of sales on ad spend, an exam item asks how much of the sales swing the ads explain, and the answer is the squared correlation, not the correlation itself.

terms.definition: The contractual penalty owed when a provider misses its service-level target — typically 10% of the monthly fee for the first missed tier, rising by band and capped at 100%. In most agreements it is the customer's sole remedy, and it must be claimed inside a stated window, often 30 days, or the right to it lapses entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-to-business account roleplay, the competitor who knows the credit must be requested rather than issued automatically recovers real money for the client.

terms.definition: Underestimating how long one's own project will take while knowing perfectly well that similar projects overran. Students who named a completion date they were 99% certain of met it only about 45% of the time. The correction is not more detail but the outside view: forecast from the distribution of comparable finished projects instead of from the steps of this plan, since added detail makes the inside view more convincing without making it more accurate.
terms.whyItMatters: Team Decision Making cases that ask for an implementation timeline are scored on defensibility, and a schedule justified by how long the last three comparable rollouts took beats a task-by-task estimate a judge can poke a hole in.

terms.definition: The smoothed yearly rate that carries a starting value to an ending value over n years: (ending value / beginning value)^(1/n) - 1. It deliberately hides year-to-year swings, so a category that jumped 40% and then fell 20% still reports one steady rate.
terms.whyItMatters: Marketing-plan questions that give a market size for two years and a span expect this exponent, not the two values subtracted and divided by the number of years.

terms.definition: Merchandise sold under the retailer's own name and sourced from a contract manufacturer, typically carrying a retail gross margin about 10 percentage points above the comparable national brand — roughly 35% against 25% — while retailing 15% to 30% cheaper, because the retailer carries no national advertising cost; the national brand by contrast is owned, advertised and priced by the manufacturer, who keeps that margin.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays about shelf space are settled with this margin arithmetic, and a competitor who argues only that the store brand is cheaper has missed why the retailer prefers it.

terms.definition: Defect count divided by units shipped, times 1,000,000: 35 rejects out of 500,000 units is 70, the scale supplier scorecards use because the same figure written as a percentage -- 0.007% -- rounds toward nothing and cannot separate a good supplier from an excellent one.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-selection roleplays hand you competing quality records; comparing them on this scale, rather than on a rounded percentage, is what makes the recommendation defensible.

terms.definition: The break-even formula with the owner's desired profit added to the numerator: (fixed costs + target profit) / contribution margin per unit. Break-even sets that target to zero, so the answer here is always the larger of the two volumes for the same cost structure.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance judge asks not whether the store survives but how many units it must sell to fund a $30,000 owner's draw, which is this calculation rather than break-even.

terms.definition: Coverage, mentions and shares a brand receives without buying placement — as against paid media, which is bought inventory the brand controls outright, and owned media, which is the brand's own site, list and channels. Only the paid third can be guaranteed to appear on a chosen date.
terms.whyItMatters: A launch-planning roleplay that leans on press pickup for a fixed launch day is the trap this term defends against, and public-relations items on the exam expect the three-way split to be named, not just the unpaid half.

terms.definition: A warehouse layout placing one central fact table of numeric measures among denormalized dimension tables, each exactly one join away from the facts; the snowflake variant normalizes those dimensions into further sub-tables, which saves storage and removes redundancy but adds a join to every query that touches them.
terms.whyItMatters: A database-design item shows a sales fact table ringed by product, store and date tables and asks why the dimensions repeat values instead of being split further.

terms.definition: The finding that a customer whose problem is fixed exceptionally well can finish more loyal than one who never had a problem — but it holds only for a first, low-severity failure resolved fast by someone empowered to fix it on the spot. On a repeat failure the effect reverses and satisfaction lands below the never-failed baseline, so engineering failures is never the strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Complaint roleplays reward naming the condition; a competitor who claims the paradox always applies is marked down for it.

terms.definition: Low performers overestimate their rank while top performers underestimate theirs, because judging one's own competence requires the very competence being judged. The popular version -- that the least able believe they are experts -- is wrong on the data: absolute self-ratings cluster near average across every quartile, the error is in relative rank, and part of the pattern is ordinary regression to the mean.
terms.whyItMatters: Business Administration Core items on assessing strengths and weaknesses use the misstatement as a distractor, and a self-evaluation roleplay is scored on whether you seek an outside measure -- a score, a manager's rating -- rather than trusting a self-estimate.

terms.definition: A written document laying out marketing objectives, strategies, and tactics for a period.
terms.whyItMatters: The plan guides all promotional and customer-facing decisions.

terms.definition: A municipal rule making uninvited door-to-door solicitation of a home unlawful, so a canvasser needs a local permit or an invitation from the occupant before knocking. Courts have upheld these ordinances, and violating one is an offense in that town even when the product, the price and the sales pitch are all perfectly legitimate.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-and-ethical selling items place a canvassing crew in a town with such an ordinance and ask what must happen first; a field-selling roleplay expects permits checked before a neighborhood route is planned.

terms.definition: The sum of the discounted lifetime values of a firm's current and future customers — the asset value of the customer base itself — which can rise while brand equity falls, as when a firm buys volume with deep discounts and wins customers who think less of the name each year; brand equity is the value held in what buyers believe about the mark, customer equity the value held in the relationships and their future cash.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked whether a discount-driven growth plan is healthy, the judged answer separates the two equities and says which one the plan is spending down.

terms.definition: The share of units clearing a step with no rework or scrap; multiplied across steps it gives rolled throughput yield, so four stations each at 95% deliver only 0.95^4 = 81.5% clean units, meaning a line whose every station reports 95% is really losing almost one unit in five.
terms.whyItMatters: Quality roleplays are scored on catching hidden rework: each station passing its own target while the finished-goods number falls short is exactly the scenario this calculation explains.

terms.definition: The share of a rebate offer's buyers who qualify but never file the paperwork, which is why a $50 mail-in rebate with 40% of buyers never claiming actually costs the manufacturer $30 per unit sold — the gap between a promotion's face value and its real cost.
terms.whyItMatters: A pricing-and-promotion roleplay comparing an instant discount against a mail-in offer of the same face value turns on this: the two look identical to the customer and cost the manufacturer very different amounts.

terms.definition: Documents and files that capture a business's transactions, operations, and decisions.
terms.whyItMatters: Accurate records are required for compliance, accountability, and historical reference.

terms.definition: The measured gap between complaints received and customers actually dissatisfied — the classic TARP studies put the share of unhappy customers who bother to complain at roughly 4 in 100, so one voiced complaint stands in for about two dozen silent defectors. A falling complaint count can therefore signal abandonment rather than improvement.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay that celebrates fewer complaints needs this correction, and it is the argument that funds proactive outreach.

terms.definition: Makes an acceptance effective the instant it is properly dispatched, while a revocation, rejection or counteroffer takes effect only when it is received — so an acceptance mailed before a revocation arrives still closes the deal. It does not apply to option contracts, where acceptance must actually reach the offeror to count.
terms.whyItMatters: Contract-timing questions give two crossing letters and ask which one controls; the dispatch-versus-receipt split is the whole answer.

terms.definition: Continuing to fund a failing course of action in order to justify having chosen it. The dividing line from the sunk-cost fallacy is who is deciding: sunk cost is the reasoning error of counting unrecoverable spend at all, and anyone can make it, while escalation is the behavioral pattern driven by personal responsibility -- managers who personally picked the losing project invest substantially more in it than managers who inherited the same project.
terms.whyItMatters: The structural fix a judge is listening for in a case about a doomed store opening is handing the continue-or-kill call to someone who did not make the original decision; recommending only 'ignore what we already spent' answers the smaller half of the problem.
